reason: An attacker sends malformed heartbeat requests and reads server memory, which can include session data or private keys. Leaks random memory chunks rather than all data, so partial.
salesperson_line: Attackers can silently pull passwords, session tokens and encryption keys out of your server's memory, with no login.

reason: The evidence shows unauthenticated MongoDB and Elasticsearch instances flagged as compromised, so anyone can read or change all their data. The host already shows signs of attacker control.
salesperson_line: Attackers have probably already taken over this system. They can read, change or delete everything on it.

reason: Automated ransom campaigns reach open databases, wipe them and leave a note. The data has already been deleted or changed.
salesperson_line: Criminals have already wiped this database and left a ransom demand. Data is likely lost and the system is wide open.

reason: Anyone can connect to MongoDB with no login and read, change or drop every database. Mass-scanning wipe-and-ransom campaigns target this exposure.
salesperson_line: Anyone on the internet can read, copy or delete your entire database without a password.

reason: An unauthenticated Redis lets an attacker read and overwrite all keys. It can also write files such as SSH keys or cron jobs through config commands, a path widely used by botnets and miners.
salesperson_line: Anyone can read or erase your Redis data and often take over the whole server with no password.

reason: An Elasticsearch server with no login lets anyone read, alter or delete every index. Wipe-and-ransom campaigns hit this exposure at scale.
salesperson_line: Anyone can read, copy or delete all the data in your search database, including customer and product records.

reason: Anyone can list and pull stored images and extract source code or embedded secrets. Pushing images might be possible too, but that is not shown, so partial. Exposed registries are documented, but I found no reports of widespread abuse.
salesperson_line: Anyone can download your company's software images, which often contain source code, passwords and keys.

reason: Anyone can log in as anonymous and read the files, and possibly upload to them. Anonymous FTP is a long-standing mass-scanned target used to steal data and host malware.
salesperson_line: Anyone can log in to your file server with no password and download, or possibly upload, files.

reason: Anyone can list the share names without a login, which shows what to target next. Access to the share contents is not demonstrated, so information.
salesperson_line: Anyone can see the names of your shared drives without logging in, which helps them plan an attack on your files.

reason: The VNC server accepts connections with security type None, so an attacker gets the remote screen, keyboard and mouse directly. Open VNC is mass-scanned and abused.
salesperson_line: Anyone can remotely see and control this computer's screen and keyboard with no password.

reason: The device's setup service returns the admin password in plaintext to an unauthenticated query, which gives admin control of the adapter. I found no reports of widespread abuse.
salesperson_line: The device hands out its admin password to anyone who asks, letting attackers reconfigure it and tamper with the equipment behind it.

reason: The printer's admin page has no password, so an attacker can change its settings, read device details and possibly pivot into the network. The control is limited to the printer.
salesperson_line: Anyone can open your printer's admin page and change its settings, which could expose scanned documents or give a foothold in your network.

reason: Anyone can send requests to the model server with no login. Attackers are reported to hijack exposed LLM endpoints to run their own workloads on the owner's hardware. The server itself is not taken over, so partial.
salesperson_line: Anyone can use your AI server for free on your hardware, read what it holds, and possibly change its models.

reason: These protocols have no authentication, so anyone reaching the port can read device data and possibly send commands. The evidence shows only identity replies, so partial. Internet-exposed ICS devices are scanned and tampered with.
salesperson_line: Anyone on the internet can talk to your industrial controllers, read their data and possibly change how your equipment runs.

reason: The private host key is publicly known, so an attacker sitting on the network path can impersonate the server and capture logins. That needs a position on the victim's network path, so it is not automatable.
salesperson_line: The server's identity key is public, so an attacker on the network path can pose as it and capture admin passwords.

reason: The listed Exchange flaws, notably the ProxyShell chain (CVE-2021-34473, 34523, 31207), allow unauthenticated remote code execution and are mass-exploited. The scanner only inferred this from the version, so it is unconfirmed.
salesperson_line: If this Exchange server is unpatched, attackers can take it over from the internet and read all company email.

reason: The gauge answers inventory commands with no authentication, and the same interface accepts configuration commands. Attacks on exposed gauges have been reported. Reading tank data is clear, while changing settings is less so, so partial.
salesperson_line: Anyone can read your fuel tank levels and possibly tamper with gauge alarms and settings, hiding leaks or theft.

reason: Anyone can list the shared module names. Whether the contents are readable without a login is not shown, so information.
salesperson_line: Anyone can see the names of your shared backup folders, and may be able to download their contents.

reason: Attackers have used internet-exposed IPMI controllers for server takeover and ransomware. IPMI 2.0 password hashes can be fetched and cracked offline, but that needs target-specific guessing, so not automatable. Control of the controller is full control of the server.
salesperson_line: Attackers can try to break into the server's hidden management controller and take full control, even when the server is powered off.

reason: Exposed ESXi and vCenter management is targeted by ransomware crews through password guessing and known flaws. The finding alone shows a reachable login, not a bypass, so not automatable. Control of the hypervisor means control of every virtual machine on it.
salesperson_line: The control panel for all your virtual servers is open to the internet. Attackers who get in can encrypt or delete every server at once.

reason: Attackers spoof a victim's address and send small monlist requests, and the server sends back much larger replies at the victim (an amplified denial of service). The reply also reveals the server's recent client addresses.
salesperson_line: Attackers can use your time server to flood other sites with traffic, and see which machines have recently talked to it.

reason: Attackers send spoofed queries so the resolver floods a victim with amplified replies. It gives no access to data or control, so information.
salesperson_line: Attackers can use your DNS server to flood other sites with traffic, getting your network blamed and slowed.

reason: Mass scanners try default community strings such as public and read device details like model, firmware and name. The description only confirms details were returned, so information.
salesperson_line: Attackers can ask your network device for its model and software details using a default password, then pick matching exploits.

reason: Ransomware crews brute-force or reuse stolen credentials against internet-facing RDP, and a successful login gives full control. The exposure alone needs a valid password, so not automatable.
salesperson_line: Attackers can keep guessing passwords on your remote desktop login. One success gives them full control of the machine.

reason: Standard RDP Security allows downgrade and man-in-the-middle attacks, with public tools such as Seth, that capture credentials. The attacker must sit on the network path, so not automatable.
salesperson_line: Remote desktop logins use an outdated, weak protection. An attacker on the network path can capture passwords and watch the session.

reason: SMBv1 is the protocol behind EternalBlue-style worms. Speaking SMBv1 alone does not show the host is unpatched, so I chose not automatable and partial.
salesperson_line: This server uses the old file-sharing protocol that WannaCry-style worms spread through, so unpatched machines can be taken over.

reason: Botnets such as Mirai scan for Telnet and try default or weak passwords, and a login gives a command shell. The login still needs a password, so I chose not automatable.
salesperson_line: Attackers can keep guessing passwords on this unencrypted remote login. If one works, they control the device.

reason: Anyone can read system metrics such as hostname, kernel and load with a plain request. This helps plan an attack but gives no control or data.
salesperson_line: Anyone can see your server's name, operating system version and load, which helps them pick the right attack.

reason: Anyone can browse the folder and download listed files, and search-engine dorks find these listings. What the files contain varies, so I chose information.
salesperson_line: Anyone can browse and download files on your website that were never meant to be public.

reason: Internet-reachable databases are brute-forced and probed for flaws. The finding only shows the port answers, not that a login is bypassed, so not automatable. Impact is partial because access still depends on credentials or a separate flaw.
salesperson_line: Your database is reachable from the internet, so attackers can keep guessing passwords or look for flaws to steal or delete data.

reason: The DICOM server accepted an association, so an attacker with standard imaging tools can query and retrieve stored scans and patient details. Large exposures of imaging servers are documented, but I found no reports of widespread abuse.
salesperson_line: Attackers may be able to search and download patient scans and personal details from this medical imaging server.

reason: POODLE and DROWN-style attacks can recover parts of encrypted traffic such as cookies. They need the attacker on the network path, so not automatable.
salesperson_line: The site still supports broken encryption. An attacker on the network path could decrypt parts of customer sessions.

reason: A 1024-bit RSA key or MD5 signature weakens the certificate, but there is no public method to break it. Exploiting it would need a network-path position and heavy computing. Impact is information as the lower choice.
salesperson_line: The site's security certificate is weaker than today's standards. A well-resourced attacker could eventually impersonate the site or read its traffic.

reason: No updates means known flaws stay open, but the finding names no specific flaw. An attacker would still need to chain a separate vulnerability.
salesperson_line: This system no longer gets security fixes, so every newly found flaw stays open for attackers to use.

reason: An unauthenticated request to the DVR web interface returns the device configuration, which can include credentials. Public exploit code exists but I found no reports of widespread abuse.
salesperson_line: Attackers can download your security-camera recorder's settings, including passwords, without logging in.

reason: A connection request with a database name starting with a hyphen can corrupt files without logging in, but code execution needs valid credentials. I chose no and partial for that reason.
salesperson_line: Attackers can crash or corrupt your PostgreSQL database, and with a valid login can take over the server.

reason: Malformed heartbeat packets make a vulnerable OpenSSL return chunks of server memory, which can include keys and session data. Widely exploited, but only random memory is returned, so partial.
salesperson_line: Attackers can silently pull passwords, session tokens and encryption keys from your server's memory without logging in.

reason: FREAK needs a man-in-the-middle to force weak export-grade RSA keys, which can then be cracked. The attacker must be on the network path.
salesperson_line: An attacker on the network path could force weak encryption and then read traffic the software thought was protected.

reason: A crafted HTTP Range header sent to HTTP.sys is widely used to crash or probe Windows web servers, and it is in CISA's exploited-vulnerabilities list. Reliable public exploits only crash the system or leak memory, so partial.
salesperson_line: Attackers can crash your Windows web server with one web request, and in the worst case run their own code.

reason: A request with illegal header characters makes Jetty return fragments of memory, which can include other users' data. A public tool exists but I found no reports of widespread abuse.
salesperson_line: Attackers can read leftover fragments of your web server's memory, which may include other users' sessions or passwords.

reason: Logjam needs a man-in-the-middle to downgrade the key exchange to 512-bit values that can be cracked. The attacker must be on the network path.
salesperson_line: An attacker on the network path could downgrade your site's encryption to a crackable level and read traffic.

reason: A long If header in a WebDAV PROPFIND request overflows a buffer in IIS 6.0 and runs attacker code. Public exploits exist and it has been exploited in the wild.
salesperson_line: Attackers can take over this old Windows web server with one crafted web request, no login needed.

reason: Requesting /common/info.cgi returns device configuration details without authentication. Those details (model, MAC, network settings) help later attacks but give no control.
salesperson_line: Anyone can pull your D-Link camera's model, network address and settings without a password, which helps target it.

reason: BlueKeep lets an unauthenticated attacker run code on an unpatched Windows RDP service with crafted requests. It has been used in real attacks, including a cryptomining campaign.
salesperson_line: Attackers can take over this Windows machine over the internet through remote desktop, with no password needed.

reason: A crafted URI makes Pulse Secure read any file with no login, including password and session data that leads to VPN takeover. Mass exploitation by many groups, including ransomware crews, is widely reported.
salesperson_line: Attackers can read any file on your VPN appliance without logging in, steal passwords, and walk into your network.

reason: Authenticated admin HTTP POSTs give root command execution on the router, and it is exploited in the wild. It needs admin access, so not automatable on its own.
salesperson_line: An attacker with the router's admin login can run any command as root and take over your network gateway.

reason: Requesting specific URLs returns the router configuration without logging in, which contains password hashes and network details. Mass scanning and exploitation have been reported.
salesperson_line: Anyone can download your router's full configuration, including password data, without logging in.

reason: A crafted SMBv3 compression message gives remote code execution on unpatched Windows. Public exploit code exists but I found no reports of widespread abuse.
salesperson_line: Attackers can take over this Windows machine over the network with a crafted file-sharing message, no login needed.

reason: ProxyLogon's first step is a server-side request forgery that bypasses login, and chained with the other flaws it gives remote code execution. Mass exploitation by many groups is documented.
salesperson_line: Attackers can take over your Exchange email server from the internet without a password and read all company email.

reason: An insecure-deserialization flaw runs code as SYSTEM. It is used as part of the ProxyLogon chain, which is mass-exploited.
salesperson_line: Attackers can run their own code with top-level rights on your Exchange email server.

reason: A file-write flaw used in the ProxyLogon chain, after the login bypass, plants a web shell for code execution. It was exploited in the wild.
salesperson_line: Attackers can plant hidden backdoor files on your Exchange email server and control it.

reason: A file-write flaw used in the ProxyLogon chain, after the login bypass, plants a web shell for code execution. It was exploited in the wild.
salesperson_line: Attackers can plant hidden backdoor files on your Exchange email server and control it.

reason: The code-execution flaw was shown at Pwn2Own, but I found no public exploit or reports of use, so I chose none and not automatable.
salesperson_line: Attackers with the right skills could run their own code on this Exchange server, though no public attack tool is known.

reason: This ProxyShell step lets an attacker write files by bypassing a security check, used with 34473 and 34523 in mass attacks. On its own it is a limited bypass, so partial.
salesperson_line: Attackers can write files onto your Exchange email server as one step of a takeover chain.

reason: ProxyShell's pre-authentication path confusion starts a chain that ends in code execution as SYSTEM. Mass exploitation, including ransomware, is reported.
salesperson_line: Attackers can take over your Exchange email server from the internet with no password and read all company email.

reason: This ProxyShell step raises an attacker to admin in Exchange PowerShell. It is part of the actively exploited chain, but is a privilege step, so partial.
salesperson_line: Attackers can turn a basic Exchange foothold into administrator rights, which lets them run commands on your email server.

reason: A path-traversal URL under /public/plugins lets anyone read any file Grafana can see, including its database and secrets. It was mass-scanned and exploited after disclosure.
salesperson_line: Anyone can read files on your Grafana server, including stored passwords and keys, with no login.

reason: An oversized username or password sent to /cgi-bin/wlogin.cgi overflows a buffer on the router with no login. A public write-up exists, but I found no confirmed reports of widespread abuse.
salesperson_line: Attackers can crash or take over this DrayTek router with one crafted login request, no password needed.

reason: An attacker who can open a streaming connection (not enabled by default) sends a crafted hostname that runs commands as the netdata user. I found no public exploit, and the attack needs streaming access.
salesperson_line: Attackers who can connect to your Netdata streaming port could run commands on the monitoring server.

reason: An attacker can use a machine's GUID as the streaming API key to send data to a Netdata parent. It only matters where streaming is enabled, and it needs the GUID.
salesperson_line: Attackers could feed fake data into your monitoring system, or get a foothold for further attacks, if streaming is switched on.

reason: Command injection through downloader.php runs system commands with no login. It is in CISA's exploited-vulnerabilities list and used by botnets.
salesperson_line: Attackers can run any command on this solar monitoring device from the internet and take it over.

reason: Spoofed proxy headers make the server treat the attacker as local, which can allow a passwordless admin login depending on account settings. I found no public exploit and success depends on configuration, so I chose lower values.
salesperson_line: Attackers may log in as administrator to your media server without a password if its accounts are left loosely set up.

reason: Unauthenticated RocketMQ components accept a config update that runs commands as the service user. It is in CISA's exploited-vulnerabilities list and used by botnets.
salesperson_line: Attackers can run their own commands on your message server over the internet with no login.

reason: An administrator can point the endpoint at an executable on a network share to run it on the server. It needs an admin account, and I found no reports of use.
salesperson_line: Someone with a Jellyfin admin account could run any program on your media server.

reason: The Jenkins CLI expands an @file argument and returns arbitrary files with no login, exposing secrets that lead to takeover. Mass exploitation, including ransomware use, is reported.
salesperson_line: Attackers can read any file on your Jenkins build server, including stored passwords and keys, without logging in.

reason: CitrixBleed 2: crafted requests to a NetScaler gateway return leftover memory, which can include session tokens. It is exploited in the wild, but only memory fragments leak, so partial.
salesperson_line: Attackers can steal logged-in session tokens from your Citrix gateway and walk into your network as real users.

reason: A crafted HTTP Range header sent to HTTP.sys is widely used to crash or probe Windows web servers, and it is in CISA's exploited-vulnerabilities list. Reliable public exploits only crash the system or leak memory, so partial.
salesperson_line: Attackers can crash your Windows web server with one web request, and in the worst case run their own code.

reason: EternalBlue sends crafted SMBv1 messages that give unauthenticated remote code execution, and it powered WannaCry and NotPetya. It is still used in the wild.
salesperson_line: Attackers can take over this Windows machine over the network with no password and spread ransomware to others.
